track.name: Linear Progression Program
track.description: The novice barbell program: three full-body sessions a week, weight on the bar every session, until it stops going up.

phase_sequence.name: Novice Linear Progression
phase_sequence.description: Squat 3×5 every session, press or bench 3×5 alternating, deadlift 1×5. Each session adds weight — about 5 lb on the squat and deadlift, 2.5 lb on the press. Conditioning stays minimal so recovery goes to the bar. The phase runs until a lift stalls for three consecutive sessions; that is the end of the novice period.
adaptations: Maximal strength in the main barbell lifts
phase_sequence.intensity: Heavy sets of five, every session

goal.notes: Strictly a novice-to-early-intermediate barbell methodology. Not designed for concurrent training; Rippetoe explicitly argues against mixing heavy conditioning with linear progression due to recovery interference. Scope limited to strength domains — this philosophy has no conditioning prescription beyond "don't do much." Novice completion benchmarks: squat 1.5× BW, deadlift 2× BW, press 0.75× BW.

archetype.name: Heavy/Light/Medium (HLM)
archetype.notes:
Rippetoe's Heavy/Light/Medium weekly variant. Three training sessions per week on the same movement patterns but at differentiated intensities: Heavy day (Monday) at 90%+, Light day (Wednesday) at 80%, Medium day (Friday) at 85%. This distributes stress and recovery across the week, allows continued practice of patterns at every session, and prevents the repeated-heavy-exposure fatigue of 3×5 run long-term. Particularly useful when the athlete has stalled on linear progression. The three slots below are parameterized for the Heavy day; intensity_pct_1rm values should be scaled by the day modifier at generation time:
  heavy_day_modifier: 1.00
  medium_day_modifier: 0.94
  light_day_modifier: 0.89

slots.notes: Heavy day: 3×5 at 90%+. Light day: 3×5 at 80%. Medium day: 3×5 at 85%.
Alternate press and bench across sessions. Intensity follows same H/L/M pattern.
Single top set deadlift. On Light day deadlift may be replaced with power clean 3×3.
Chin-ups or rows. Present on all three days; load does not vary with H/L/M.

deload.notes: Convert all three sessions to Light-day intensity (80%) and reduce sets to 2 per lift.

time_limited.notes: Drop accessory upper work. The three primary slots are non-negotiable for HLM integrity.

substitutions.substitute_approach: Cannot perform back squat. Substitute goblet squat or trap bar DL for lower. Floor press replaces bench.

goal.name: Horsemen GPP / SOF-Style Training

track.name: 4-Month Macro
track.description: The source's four months — strength, power endurance, job specific, maintenance — each a 28-day template started on the 1st of the month, with the days left over free, and the whole run two or three times. Every week is six training days and a rest day. The strength and conditioning numbers the source names are what it aims to reach in four months.

phase_sequence.name: Strength
phase_sequence.description: Month one: strength twice a week, on days 1 and 5; a job-specific day, a power-endurance day and one rotating day (SMMF, power, a progression workout or a circuit) between them; recovery on day 6 and rest on day 7. Strength days work up to a 1RM in the day's lift, then percentages of it, then accessory rounds; there is no RPE. The source lists the PT test among its hard job-specific options and never schedules it; here it takes the month's first hard job-specific day (week 2) as a baseline for the four-month goals.
adaptations: Maximal strength toward the bodyweight goals
Power endurance and job-specific capacity kept alongside it
phase_sequence.intensity: Heavy: a 1RM worked up to on the day, then percentages of it

phase_sequence.name: Power Endurance
phase_sequence.description: Month two puts power endurance first — about four sessions every two weeks: runs with get-ups, the Secret Service Snatch Test, Tabata, a 5K row, EMOMs. Strength drops to maintenance, about twice in two weeks, beside job-specific days, an endurance session of 60 minutes or more, recovery and a rest day each week.

phase_sequence.name: Job Specific
phase_sequence.description: Month three makes job-specific days most of the week: climbing and grip work, leg blasters, a ruck run, the PT tests, tire and sled work. Strength and power endurance alternate around them, with recovery on day 6 and rest on day 7.

phase_sequence.name: Maintenance
phase_sequence.description: Month four holds what the macro built: recovery twice a week at 65% of max heart rate or less, circuits, strength, and a hard job-specific day, with rest on day 7. The PT test, one of the source's hard job-specific options, takes the macro's last hard job-specific day: the most rested point of the four months, and the check against their goals.
phase_sequence.intensity: Hard days between recovery at ≤65% max HR

goal.notes: Written by "the Horsemen" for special-operations operators ("Team guys") to build a broad operator base of fitness. It states no prerequisites and has no novice path; daily 1RM work, Olympic lifts at 80-100% and gymnastics such as handstand push-ups and rope climbs assume an experienced athlete. Its numbers are goals to reach within four months, not entry standards: deadlift 2.5x, front squat 1.5x, bench press 1.5x and military press 1.0x bodyweight, 3 miles in under 20:00, and at least 200 on the Secret Service Snatch Test (SSST). The PT test is a separate list: max pull-ups (minimum 15), sit-ups in 3 minutes (90), push-ups in 3 minutes (80), a 3-mile run (22:30) and an 800 m swim (14:30). The program is four 28-day months — strength, power endurance, job specific, maintenance — run two or three times. Every week is six sessions and a rest day, with recovery days (30-60 minutes at 65% of max heart rate or less) built in. Each day is a category — strength, power endurance, job specific, SMMF, progression, circuits, density, accumulation, endurance or recovery — and the workout is picked from that category's list of named workouts. Loads come from a 1RM worked up to on the day, then percentages of it, fixed loads or multiples of bodyweight; there is no RPE and no deload week. The 4-Month Macro track runs the source as written: each month's week templates day by day, every named workout as an archetype in its category's pool, taken in rotation, and prescribed exactly as the source writes it (src/week_template.py). A workout whose equipment the athlete lacks is passed over for the next one; names carrying profanity or a slur are cleaned.
